articles.title: Funeral Tents, Altars and Ghost Money: What You Are Seeing on a Vietnamese Street
articles.excerpt: A tent across the lane, music at four in the morning, paper money burning in a bin on the pavement. These are the most visible pieces of Vietnamese religious life, and here is what each one means and how to behave around it.
articles.content:
Within a day of arriving in Vietnam you will see something you cannot read: a canopy blocking a side street with a crowd in white headbands under it, a tray of fruit and burning incense on the pavement outside a phone shop, a fire of printed paper in a tin bucket, a brass band at an hour when no band should be playing. Guidebooks list temples and pagodas. The religion most visitors actually encounter is this one, practised at home and on the street, and it is easy to understand once someone explains it.

The altars

Almost every Vietnamese home and business keeps an altar, and it is the first thing to recognise. The ancestor altar inside the house holds photographs of the dead, incense, fruit, tea and sometimes cigarettes or a glass of liquor, and it is where the family marks anniversaries and the lunar new year.

The low altar at floor level by the door of a shop, with a fat laughing figure, a red lamp and offerings, is for the god of wealth and the god of the land, and it is tended every morning for business.

The belief underneath both is that the dead and the spirits need the same things the living do, food, money, cigarettes, a drink, and that a household looks after its own. It is older than Buddhism in Vietnam and it sits alongside it; a family can be Buddhist, Catholic or nothing in particular and still keep the ancestors fed.

What to do

Nothing, except not to step over an offering left on the pavement and not to point your feet at an altar if you are sitting near one. If you are a guest in a home, a glance at the ancestor altar and a small nod is noticed and appreciated. Photographs of a shop altar are fine; photographs of a family at theirs are not, unless invited.

The paper money

The printed paper being burned in a bucket on the pavement is money for the dead: imitation banknotes, often printed to look like US dollars, along with paper versions of clothes, houses, motorbikes and phones, sent to the ancestors by fire. It is burned on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, at the new year, on death anniversaries and heavily during the seventh lunar month, when the dead are believed to walk.

The practice is shared across Chinese-influenced East and Southeast Asia; Vietnam's version is its own.

Charred notes blow along the streets after a burning. People will tell you not to pick them up or keep one, because the money belongs to the dead and keeping it is bad luck. Whether or not you hold the belief, it is a courtesy to leave it where it fell.

The shops that sell it

Whole streets sell nothing else, most famously in Hanoi's Old Quarter on the street named for paper goods. The paper houses and cars are a craft in their own right and are worth a look as objects; buying one as a joke is the kind of thing that reads worse than it was meant.

The funeral tent

A canopy across a residential lane, with chairs, a portrait on a draped altar, a coffin inside the house and a family in white headbands, is a funeral, held at home over several days before the burial or cremation. The house receives visitors through the day and night, the family keeps vigil, and the neighbourhood accepts the closed street as a matter of course. Mourning clothes are white, not black; the headband marks the relationship to the dead.

The music is the part that wakes visitors. Funeral bands play at intervals through the night and, in the south especially, brass instruments and drums go with the procession, which leaves before dawn to avoid the heat and the traffic. A hearse decorated with dragons and a crowd on foot behind it at five in the morning is the funeral leaving. Lanterns, paper and firecrackers are not; those are the new year.

What to do

Walk around the tent, not through it, lower your voice, and do not photograph the coffin or the family. If you are staying nearby and the music keeps you up, that is a night, and a tourist's complaint to a grieving family is the one thing that would genuinely cause offence. If you knew the person, a white envelope with a modest amount of money, handed to the family with both hands, is the custom.

The anniversary party

The gathering you may be invited to as a guest of a family is a death anniversary, called a giỗ, and it is a party rather than a wake. Vietnamese families mark the date of a relative's death, not their birthday, with a meal in which the first dishes are placed on the altar for the ancestor before the living eat.

Relatives come from a distance, there is a lot of food, and a foreign guest is a welcome addition rather than an intrusion.

Bring fruit or something for the table, eat what you are given, and expect to be offered rice liquor by the older men. There is no mourning in the room. The dead are present as a guest of honour, and the point of the day is the family in the same house.

Tombs in the fields

The ornate little structures standing in rice paddies and on hillsides across the countryside are family tombs, placed on the family's land and visited at the new year and on anniversaries. In the central provinces around Hue some are elaborate enough to pass for small temples. Nobody minds you looking from the road.

Reading the calendar

Most of what you see follows the lunar calendar rather than the Western one. Offerings and burnings peak on the first and the fifteenth of each lunar month; the seventh month is the month of the dead, with the biggest burnings and the most street altars; the days before Tet are a general cleaning of altars and graves and a time of heavy incense.

A lunar calendar app, or a glance at the small lunar date printed on Vietnamese calendars, tells you why the street is suddenly full of smoke.

None of this requires anything of you beyond stepping carefully and keeping the camera down at the right moments. It rewards attention, because once the pieces have names, the ordinary street turns out to be where most of Vietnam's religious life is happening.

articles.title: Returning to Vietnam as a Vietnamese American: Papers, Family and the First Trip Back
articles.excerpt: A first trip back has questions the tourist articles do not answer: which visa, which passport, what Vietnam considers your children to be, and how to stay with family. Here is the practical layer under the emotional one.
articles.content:
Vietnamese Americans are the largest group of US travellers to Vietnam with a reason beyond tourism: a first trip back, a family visit, a parent's grave, a cousin's wedding, a child being shown where the family came from. The trip has an emotional layer this site cannot plan for you. It also has a paperwork layer that is different from an ordinary American's and that trips up a surprising number of families at the airport, and that is what this article covers.

Which visa, or none

A Vietnamese American travelling on a US passport needs a visa to enter Vietnam like any other American, with one route the tourist articles mention only in passing. Under Decree 82/2015, overseas Vietnamese and their foreign spouses and children can apply for a visa-exemption paper valid for up to five years, with a six-month stay on each entry, instead of a visa for each trip.

For a family that will go back more than once, it replaces the e-visa and its ninety-day limit with something closer to a standing permission.

Eligibility is proved with a document showing Vietnamese origin: a Vietnamese birth certificate, a decision renouncing Vietnamese nationality, a certificate of loss of nationality, or another paper stating former nationality; a spouse or child of an overseas Vietnamese proves the relationship instead. The passport must have at least a year left when you apply. Applications from the United States go through a Vietnamese consulate; the paper can also be applied for in Vietnam at the Immigration Department.

If you are going once

The ordinary e-visa, up to 90 days, is simpler for a single trip and needs no proof of origin. Ask for the full length you might want, because Vietnam does not allow you to renew or extend an e-visa while you are in the country. Which of the two routes fits your family's pattern of trips is one of the visa decisions the complete Vietnam decision manual lays out side by side.

Which passport

If you or a family member holds both a US and a Vietnamese passport, the rule is fixed: you must enter and exit Vietnam on the same passport, and travel domestically on the passport you entered with. Entering on the Vietnamese passport and flying home on the American one, or the reverse, is the error that strands people at departure.

Decide which passport the trip runs on before you book, and use it for every domestic flight too, because airlines check.

Vietnamese nationality is not lost simply by becoming an American citizen. The decree's own list of proofs includes a formal decision renouncing it, which tells you that renunciation is a process rather than a side effect. Someone who left as a child and never renounced may still be a Vietnamese national in Vietnamese law, with consequences for their children that the next section covers.

Your children

Children of Vietnamese parentage are the part of the paperwork most families do not see coming. The US Embassy states that in general a Vietnamese passport or a Vietnamese exit visa is required by the Vietnamese government in the event your child needs to exit Vietnam. The requirement attaches to parentage, not to the passport the child entered on. In practice this is raised at departure rather than arrival, which is the worst place to discover it.

The State Department adds a second rule for children travelling without both parents: notarised consent is required for every Vietnamese minor, including dual US citizens, to travel without a parent or guardian, and Vietnamese authorities have sometimes stopped US-citizen minors from leaving without it. A grandparent taking a grandchild to the village, or one parent travelling alone with the children, should carry the other parent's notarised consent letter or proof of sole custody.

What to do before you fly

Ask the Vietnamese consulate, before booking, how your child's parentage is treated and what document they want at exit. The US Embassy cannot help with this; it is a Vietnamese government question, and the consulate's answer is the one that counts at the airport.

Staying with family

Staying with relatives rather than in a hotel is normal and it has one administrative step. every visitor must have their overnight address registered with the local police; hotels do it automatically, and in a family home the duty is the host's: by law the host must declare a foreign guest's temporary residence to the local police within 12 hours of arrival, or 24 hours in remote areas, usually online.

Mention it to your relatives on the first evening. Most know the drill, and the ward police office is a familiar place to them.

Relatives will also expect gifts, and will have views on what you should bring: American vitamins, cosmetics and branded goods remain the classic requests, and cash in envelopes for the older generation is the custom. Prices inside Vietnam are set in dong by law, so change or withdraw a sensible amount early rather than arriving with a wallet of small US notes.

The altar and the graves

A first visit usually includes the family altar and the family tombs, and relatives will guide you through the incense and the bows. The anniversary of a death, not a birthday, is the family gathering, and if your trip can be timed to a parent's or grandparent's giỗ, the family will be assembled for you.

Timing and flights

The weeks before Tet are the peak for flights from the United States, because so many families fly back for the new year, and the fares and the crowds reflect it. Tet falls on 6 February 2027, and a trip timed to it means booking months ahead and accepting that the country closes for the holiday week. A trip in the dry, cool months either side of it gets the family without the squeeze.

The only nonstop flight is Vietnam Airlines' San Francisco to Ho Chi Minh City flight; from Orange County, San Jose, Houston or Seattle the choice is that flight via the Bay Area or a one-stop through an Asian hub, and the one-stops are often cheaper and land in Hanoi or Da Nang directly if the family is in the north or the centre.

Being Việt kiều

Overseas Vietnamese were once resented at home and are now courted, officially and by the market, and both attitudes survive. You may be charged the local price or the foreigner's price depending on your accent; relatives may assume wealth; a younger cousin may know more of the music you grew up with, through the diaspora variety shows, than you expect. The language is the other surprise: a Vietnamese learned at home in California is often a southern Vietnamese of the 1970s, and relatives will hear it. None of this spoils the trip, and most returning families say the thing they did not expect was how ordinary, and how welcoming, the country was.

articles.title: Why Every Vietnamese City Has the Same Street Names
articles.excerpt: Hai Ba Trung, Tran Hung Dao, Le Loi, Nguyen Hue. The same dozen names run through every town in Vietnam because they are a history lesson painted on signs. Here is who they were.
articles.content:
Spend a week in Vietnam and the street names start to repeat. You stayed on Le Loi in Hue, crossed Tran Hung Dao in Hanoi, and now Ho Chi Minh City has both, plus a Hai Ba Trung, a Nguyen Hue and a Ly Thuong Kiet, which you are sure were in Da Nang as well. They were. Vietnamese cities name their main streets after the same set of national heroes, in a pattern that was deliberate, and learning a dozen of them turns every city map into a short course in two thousand years of resisting invasion.

The pattern and where it came from

Vietnamese street names are drawn from a national list of heroes, dynasties, battles and dates, applied city by city after independence, so that the same names recur from Hanoi to the delta. The French had named the streets after French soldiers and administrators. After 1954 in the north and 1975 in the south, those names were replaced with Vietnamese ones, and the ones chosen were the figures a unified country wanted everyone to know.

The result is that the biggest street in most towns is named for a general who defeated the Chinese or the Mongols.

The pattern is not identical everywhere. Hanoi's Old Quarter keeps its medieval guild names, Ho Chi Minh City keeps a few French scientists, and every town adds its own local heroes. But the core list is national, and you will see it on every map.

How to read an address

Vietnamese addresses put the house number first and the street name after it, and an address with a slash, such as 123/4, means house 4 in the alley that opens at number 123. The word for street, đường or phố, often appears before the name on signs and is dropped in speech.

The ancient resistance

Hai Ba Trung, the Trung sisters, led a revolt against Chinese rule in the year 40 and ruled for about three years before the Chinese returned; their name is on a major street in every city and they are the emblem of Vietnamese nationhood and of its women. Ba Trieu, a woman who led another rising two centuries later, usually has a street nearby.

Ngo Quyen won the battle on the Bach Dang river in 938 that ended a thousand years of Chinese rule, and his name marks that ending.

Hung Vuong, the legendary founding kings, give their name to the broad ceremonial avenue in many towns, and to the public holiday in the spring when the nation commemorates them.

The dynasties

Ly Thai To founded Thang Long, today's Hanoi, as the capital in 1010, and his statue stands beside the lake there. Ly Thuong Kiet was his dynasty's great general against the Song. Tran Hung Dao turned back three Mongol invasions in the thirteenth century, the last with the same trick of stakes in the Bach Dang river, and his is perhaps the most universal street name of all. Le Loi drove out the Ming in the 1420s, and Nguyen Trai was the scholar and strategist beside him. Le Thanh Ton, the Le dynasty's greatest emperor, extended the country south into Champa in the fifteenth century.

The eighteenth century and the French

Nguyen Hue and Quang Trung are the same man: the Tay Son brother who united the country in the 1780s and routed a Chinese army at Tet in 1789, and who took Quang Trung as his reign name. Ho Chi Minh City's grand pedestrian boulevard is named for him under one name and other cities use the other.

Phan Boi Chau and Phan Chu Trinh were the early twentieth-century nationalists who argued, in different ways, for ending French rule; their streets are often side by side.

A few French names survived the purge. Pasteur, whose institutes still operate in Vietnam, and Yersin, who worked in Nha Trang and founded Dalat, kept their streets in Ho Chi Minh City because they were doctors rather than soldiers. Alexandre de Rhodes, the Jesuit credited with the Romanised script Vietnamese is written in, has a street by the Saigon cathedral.

The Old Quarter's exception

Hanoi's thirty-six streets begin with Hang, meaning merchandise, followed by what the guild once sold: Hang Gai for silk, Hang Ma for paper offerings, Hang Bac for silver. Some still sell it. These are the oldest street names in Vietnam and the only common set that is about trade rather than heroes.

The twentieth century on the signs

The modern names are dates and revolutionaries. Dien Bien Phu is the 1954 battle that ended French rule. Cach Mang Thang Tam is the August Revolution of 1945. Streets named 3 Thang 2 mark the founding of the Communist Party on 3 February 1930, and 30 Thang 4 marks 30 April 1975, the day Saigon fell.

Le Duan was the party's leader through the war and after; Vo Nguyen Giap was its general; Vo Thi Sau and Nguyen Van Troi were young resistance fighters executed by the French and the South respectively. A traveller who can read these dates can read the politics of the sign.

The Saigon renamings

Ho Chi Minh City's central streets changed names after 1975, and older Vietnamese Americans may know them by the old ones. Tu Do, the bar street of the war years, became Dong Khoi; Cong Ly became Nam Ky Khoi Nghia. Asking a relative for directions to a street that no longer exists on the map is a common first-trip experience for returning families, and a prewar map of the city, sold as a reproduction, settles most of it.

What to do with this

Use it as a mnemonic. Tran Hung Dao is usually a major artery, Le Loi and Nguyen Hue usually run through the centre, Hai Ba Trung is never far away, and the Hang streets mean you are in Hanoi's oldest quarter. The names also explain the statues: the mounted general in the square by the Saigon river is Tran Hung Dao, pointing at the water where his stakes went in.

Once you can read the signs, the cities stop being interchangeable and start telling you, in the same order, the same story.
